pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 10–11 (META): use estimation to CHECK answers to calculations, and judge, in context, an appropriate degree of accuracy. This is a monitoring/self-regulation skill layered over computation, not a new calculation method.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y6): 'use estimation to check answers to calculations and determine, in the context of a problem, an appropriate degree of accuracy'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 4.OA.3 'assess the reasonableness of answers using mental computation and estimation strategies including rounding'; supported by 5.NBT.4 rounding and SMP MP1 (make sense) / MP6 (attend to precision).
• Operational details — the child rounds each number to a convenient value (487×23 → 500×20 = 10000), computes the easy estimate, then compares it to the exact answer to catch gross errors (misplaced digit, wrong operation). Separately, they judge how precise the answer needs to be (money to 2dp, people rounded up, a fair 'about' for a crowd). Emphasis on whether the estimate is above/below and why.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 10): estimate 487×23 by rounding to 500×20 and use it to sanity-check a given answer. Tier B (10–11): spot an unreasonable answer (e.g. decimal point misplaced) by comparing with a quick estimate. Tier C (11): decide whether an exact answer or an estimate is appropriate for a given real context and justify the degree of accuracy.
bestPractices: Teach estimation as a HABIT that brackets the real calculation — estimate first (what should it be about?), compute, then compare — so it becomes automatic self-checking, not an extra chore done only when asked.

Make the purpose catching ERRORS: give calculations with planted mistakes (decimal-point slips, wrong operation, digit dropped) and have children use an estimate to flag the unreasonable ones — the estimate's job is to be roughly right, fast.
Discuss DIRECTION of rounding: rounding both factors up over-estimates, both down under-estimates — so children can say whether the true answer should be a bit more or less than the estimate.

Separate 'estimate to check' from 'degree of accuracy in context': explore contexts where over/under-estimating matters (buying enough paint = round up; sharing money = exact) so accuracy is a contextual judgement.

Value a good estimate even when 'wrong': stress it need not match the exact answer — it must be close enough to reveal a blunder; discourage children from 'estimating' by computing exactly then rounding.
keyRepresentations: Rounded-calculation shorthand: 487 × 23 ≈ 500 × 20 = 10000, written above the exact working as a check line.
Number line showing the estimate and the exact answer as nearby points — a wildly distant exact answer flags an error.
'Reasonable / unreasonable' sorting frame comparing computed answers against a quick estimate.
Up/down rounding arrows on each factor to reason whether the estimate is an over- or under-estimate.
commonMisconceptions: Computing the exact answer first and then 'rounding it' — defeating the purpose of a quick independent check.
Believing an estimate is 'wrong' unless it equals the exact answer, so distrusting the whole method.
Rounding to unhelpful values (rounding 23 to 23, or over-rounding so the estimate is useless).
Not using the estimate to actually CHECK — producing it then ignoring an exact answer that clearly conflicts.
Confusing 'appropriate accuracy' — giving money to 3dp, or rounding a count of buses down when you need enough for everyone.

learn.summary: For ages 10–11: use estimation as a habit for checking calculations and judging an appropriate degree of accuracy in context. This is a monitoring/self-regulation skill layered over computation — estimate first, compute, then compare to catch gross errors (misplaced decimal points, wrong operation, dropped digit) and decide how precise an answer needs to be for the real situation.

activities.title: Estimate Detective: flag the unreasonable answer
feedback: If the learner computes the exact answer first then rounds it, point out this defeats the purpose — the check must be a fast, independent estimate made before or instead of trusting the exact product.
When a proposed answer sits far from the estimate, confirm that the gap itself is the signal: they can flag the error without finishing the exact calculation.
If they distrust an estimate because it does not equal the exact answer, reassure that a good estimate need only be close enough to reveal a blunder.

Handle direction carefully: here 487 rounds UP to 500 but 23 rounds DOWN to 20, so this mixed-direction estimate leans both ways and its direction is not predetermined. In fact the true answer 11201 lands ABOVE the estimate 10000 (the down-rounding of 23 outweighed the up-rounding of 487), which shows why you should not assume 'rounded up means over-estimate' for a mixed case — use a both-up or both-down example when you want a clean over- or under-estimate.
activities.rationale: Estimation-to-check is a predict-then-compare loop; letting the learner set rounded factors, generate an estimate, and compare it against a proposed answer rehearses the checking habit directly. Planted errors (decimal slips, wrong operation) make the catching purpose concrete.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils use estimation to check answers to calculations and determine, in the context of a problem, an appropriate degree of accuracy.
Pupils assess the reasonableness of answers to multistep problems using mental computation and estimation strategies including rounding.
learnerActions: Face a calculation with a proposed answer, e.g. 487 × 23 with a candidate answer shown — some candidates are correct, others sabotaged by a misplaced decimal point or a wrong operation.
Round each number to a convenient, friendly value (e.g. 487 → 500, 23 → 20) and compute the easy estimate (500 × 20 = 10000).
Place the estimate and the proposed answer as points on the same number line, then judge whether the proposed answer is 'reasonable' or 'unreasonable' by how far it sits from the estimate.

State the general direction rule — rounding BOTH factors up over-estimates (so the true answer is a bit less than the estimate) and rounding BOTH down under-estimates (so the true answer is a bit more) — then notice that the 500 × 20 example is MIXED (487 rounds up, 23 rounds down), so its direction is NOT cleanly predetermined; for a mixed case rely on the estimate's MAGNITUDE to catch gross errors rather than declaring a precise over- or under-estimate.
Rule each proposed answer reasonable or not WITHOUT computing the exact product first.
activities.intendedInsight: A quick independent estimate shows roughly what size the answer should be, so an answer sitting far from the estimate is visibly wrong (487 × 23 cannot be 1121 when the estimate is ~10000). The estimate's job is to be roughly right, fast — not to match exactly.

activities.title: How accurate does it need to be?
feedback: If a learner always prefers exact answers, raise a context (roughly enough seats? approximate cost?) where speed and a ballpark beat spurious precision.
If they round a count down when more is needed, walk through the real consequence (not enough buses/paint) so the direction of rounding is tied to purpose.
Praise reasoning that fits precision to purpose, e.g. money kept to 2dp but a crowd quoted to the nearest hundred.
activities.rationale: Separating 'estimate to check' from 'degree of accuracy in context' lets learners treat accuracy as a judgement driven by the situation and its consequences rather than a mechanical rule.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils use estimation to check answers to calculations and determine, in the context of a problem, an appropriate degree of accuracy.
learnerActions: Meet real contexts — buying enough paint, sharing money fairly, counting a crowd, working out how many buses are needed — and decide whether an exact answer or an estimate is appropriate.
Choose the sensible precision for each: money to 2 decimal places, the number of buses or tins of paint needed rounded UP so there is enough, a fair 'about' for a crowd size.
Explain the consequence of choosing wrongly, e.g. rounding the number of buses down leaves people without a seat; giving money to 3 decimal places is spurious precision.
Name a situation where a rough estimate is actually more useful than an exact answer (when a ballpark is enough, or when speed matters more than precision).
activities.intendedInsight: Appropriate accuracy is a contextual judgement, not a fixed rule: the purpose of the answer sets how precise it must be, and sometimes a fast ballpark beats an exact figure.

activities.title: Does that seem about right? — reasoning aloud
feedback: If a learner says 'the estimate was 10,000 and I got 11,201 so it's definitely correct', discuss the limit: an estimate rules out gross errors but cannot confirm exactness — pair it with an inverse check when exactness matters.

If a learner dismisses estimation as pointless once the exact answer exists, show a worked example with a slipped digit (e.g. a wrong result of 1,120 offered for 487 × 23, whose true value is 11,201) that the estimate instantly flags; estimation guards against your own errors.
There is no single scored answer here — surface and value the child's reasoning rather than marking it right or wrong.
activities.rationale: The objective is metacognitive — the child's stance toward estimation as a checking tool and toward appropriate accuracy, not a computed value. Socratic prompting suits surfacing and challenging that stance; it works alongside, not instead of, the active predict/compare drill.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils use estimation to check answers to calculations and determine, in the context of a problem, an appropriate degree of accuracy.
learnerActions: Be presented with suspicious proposed answers and, before any reveal, say whether each seems about right and why.
Answer probing questions: 'If your estimate was 10,000 and your worked answer was 1,150, which do you trust — and what do you do next?'
Explain whether an estimate can ever PROVE an exact answer is 100% correct, and why not.
Describe how you would round 487 × 23 to check it, and justify why you rounded that way.
activities.intendedInsight: Estimation is a stance toward reasonableness and its limits: it can rule out place-value-sized errors but cannot verify the last digits, so it complements — not replaces — an exact or inverse check.

constraints: This is a META/self-regulation objective layered over computation, not a new calculation method — learners should already be able to perform the underlying multiplication/division.

Multiple-choice or matching tasks ('is this answer reasonable?', match calculations to best estimates, pick appropriate accuracy for a context) can assess the judgement, but recognition-only formats do not elicit the estimate-FIRST habit; include tasks where the learner generates the estimate independently.

A static annotated worked check (≈ line above the exact working, with reveal of how it exposes a decimal-point error) is a useful reference, but the checking habit is rehearsed through an active compare loop rather than by reading a fixed example.
Discourage 'estimating' by computing the exact answer and then rounding it — the check must be fast and independent.
Avoid rounding to unhelpful values (e.g. leaving 23 as 23, or over-rounding so the estimate is useless); the estimate must be both easy and close enough to reveal a blunder.

The both-factors-up/both-factors-down over/under rule only applies cleanly when both factors round the SAME way; a mixed-direction rounding (e.g. 500 × 20, where 487 rounds up and 23 rounds down) does not predetermine whether the true answer is above or below the estimate, so use magnitude for error-catching there.
An estimate rules out gross errors but cannot verify exactness; do not teach it as a guarantee of a correct answer.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source worked example '487 × 23 = 1,120' appears in an error-pattern as a planted slipped-digit mistake; the true product is 11,201. This is intentional in the diagnostic context (an unreasonable answer to be flagged), so it is retained only as an error-to-catch, never presented as correct.

Self-audit of the estimate: 500 × 20 = 10,000 is correct; the exact 487 × 23 = 11,201. Because 487 rounds up but 23 rounds down, the estimate is mixed-direction; here it lands about 11% BELOW the true value, so the simple 'rounded up ⇒ over-estimate' inference does not hold for this example. The candidate values 1,121/1,150/1,120 are correctly characterised as unreasonable.

Asking a 10–11 learner to determine which rounding 'dominates' in a mixed case was reframed to recognising that mixed roundings do not predetermine the direction; this keeps the point age-appropriate and avoids implying a clean over/under verdict for 500×20.
The second cited US standard (CCSS-M 4.OA.3) is marked verified:false in the source; do not treat its support as independently confirmed.

Optional interaction examples from the source (dial/spinner to set rounded factors, auto-computed estimate, number-line comparison, up/down arrows tinting over/under-estimate, context-consequence mode) are retained as illustrative affordances, not mandatory mechanisms.

probeDeeper: If your estimate was 10,000 and your worked answer was 1,150, which do you trust — and what does that tell you to do next?
Can an estimate ever prove your exact answer is 100% correct? Why or why not?
Give me a real situation where a rough estimate is actually better than an exact answer.
How would you round 487 × 23 to check it, and why round that way?
assess.correctAnswer: There is no single right answer to score — surface the child's thinking. Strong reasoning: round to 500 × 20 = 10,000, so a calculated answer near 11,000 is plausible but 1,100 or 110,000 is definitely wrong; the estimate can't confirm exactness but can catch place-value-sized errors. And an estimate is more useful than exactness when a ballpark is enough (is there enough money? roughly how many buses?) or when speed matters more than precision.

errorPatterns.pattern: sees estimation as pointless once an exact answer exists — 'why estimate if I can just work it out?'
errorPatterns.nextMove: surface, don't score: discuss a worked example with a slipped digit (487×23 = 1,120) that the estimate instantly flags; estimation guards against your own errors.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child dismisses estimation, treating the exact calculation as self-evidently trustworthy

errorPatterns.pattern: thinks an estimate can CONFIRM an answer is exactly right, not just flag it as reasonable
errorPatterns.nextMove: discuss the limit of estimation: it rules out gross errors but cannot verify the last digits; pair it with an inverse check for exactness.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child says 'the estimate was 10,000 and I got 11,201 so it's definitely correct'

errorPatterns.pattern: believes an exact answer is always preferable — no sense that context sets the needed accuracy
errorPatterns.nextMove: raise contexts (roughly enough seats? approximate cost?) where speed and a ballpark beat spurious precision; accuracy should fit the purpose.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child cannot name a situation where a rough answer suffices or is better

responseLevels.gap: dismisses estimation as pointless, or cannot use it to judge whether an answer is reasonable.
responseLevels.full: uses estimation to flag unreasonable answers (while recognising it can't verify exactness), and judges when a ballpark versus an exact answer fits the context, explaining the reasoning.
responseLevels.partial: uses estimation to get a ballpark but treats it as confirming exactness, or cannot articulate when approximate accuracy is more appropriate than exact.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: You worked out 487 × 23 and got an answer. Before we trust it — how could a quick estimate tell you whether the answer is probably right or definitely wrong? And when is a rough estimate actually MORE useful than an exact answer? Talk me through your thinking.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: This META objective is about the child's stance toward estimation as a checking TOOL and toward appropriate accuracy — not a computed value. The probe surfaces whether they see estimation as a way of judging reasonableness (and its limits) versus treating it as just 'a rough sum' or as pointless once you have the exact answer.
